name: As
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Arnold, Laura. 2020. Four undocumented languages of Raja Ampat, West Papua, Indonesia. In Peter K. Austin (ed.), Language Documentation and Description 17, 25-43. London: EL Publishing. doi:10.25894/LDD95
catalog_locator: pp. 27-28, section 1 'Introduction' (typological overview of the four surveyed languages Salawati, Batta, Biga and As; the sentence breaks across the page turn at 'word-final | syllables)')
catalog_quote: Typologically, all four of the surveyed languages are very similar. While the segmental inventories are quite simple (distinguishing 14-16 consonants, and five or six vowels), the four languages additionally have systems of lexical tone (typically distinguishing two or three tones on word-final syllables).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: Arnold, Laura. 2020. Four undocumented languages of Raja Ampat, West Papua, Indonesia. In Peter K. Austin (ed.), Language Documentation and Description 17, 25-43. London: EL Publishing. doi:10.25894/LDD95
new_statements.locator: pp. 27-28 (section 1, typological overview of the four surveyed languages: Salawati, Batta, Biga, As); PDF pages 4-5
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (20 pp., text; extracted text). The quoted sentence is present verbatim, beginning on p. 27 (p. 4, last paragraph of section 1) and finishing on p. 28 (p. 5, first line): "Typologically, all four of the surveyed languages are very similar. While the segmental inventories are quite simple (distinguishing 14-16 consonants, and five or six vowels), the four languages additionally have systems of lexical tone (typically distinguishing two or three tones on word-final syllables)." Footnote 5 on p. 28 adds that tone is common in Raja Ampat (Ambel, Matbat, Ma'ya tonal) and cannot be reconstructed to proto-SHWNG. Nothing in the paper mentions stress or accent for As; the only other prosody-r…
new_statements.rule_in_words: As is reported to be a lexical-tone language, with two or three tones contrasting on the word-final syllable; the source says nothing about word stress. Corroborated first-hand by Kamholz 2017 (NUSA 62, p. 8 fn. 2, saved file): 'I conducted preliminary fieldwork in 2015 on the Raja Ampat languages Biga, Batta, and As, and found apparent tonal minimal pairs in all three.'
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is hedged ('typically') and generic over the four surveyed languages, with no As-specific tone data or minimal pairs printed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical tone on word-final syllables). Based on Arnold's 2019 survey wordlists; the paper is a survey report, not a phonological description. The As section itself (pp. 37-39) is sociolinguistic only.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the As of Asbaken village (north coast of the Bird's Head, Sausapor/Makbon area), the only surviving variety; Berry & Berry 1987 also name Malaumkarta and Mega, where Arnold 2020 reports it no longer spoken. Same glottocode asss1237; no dialect split is described.

tone_statements.citation: Arnold, Laura. 2024. Lexical comparanda for 14 Austronesian varieties of Raja Ampat, northwest New Guinea [dataset, Excel workbook RA-TonalCorrespondences-vFinal.xlsx: MASTER sheet of 489 comparanda / 354 concepts with tone and stress marked, plus two analysis sheets]. Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.13859485 (v2: doi:10.5281/zenodo.14716166; concept doi:10.5281/zenodo.13859484). CC-BY 4.0.
tone_statements.quote: I use superscript numerals throughout the worksheets to represent phonological tone. Lower numbers mark lower tone, thus: ¹ (Low tone), ¹² (Rise), ³ (High), ⁴ (Extra‑High), and so forth. ... In As and the Maˈya-Salawati languages, cell colour marks the following specifications: blue = final stress, Extra High tone; green = final stress; High tone, orange = final stress, Rise tone; red = final stress, Low tone; yellow = penultimate stress, High tone (regularly corresponding to penultimate stress, Rise tone in Misool Maˈya); grey = toneless.
tone_statements.locator: Zenodo record 13859485 landing-page Description (notation paragraph; MASTER colour key)
tone_statements.summary: As forms coded with 3 tones on the word-final syllable: High (³), Low (¹), Rise (¹²); a few toneless; stress mark rare (3/123 cells); heavy inter-speaker variation.

sources.citation: Berry, Keith & Christine Berry. 1987. A survey of some West Papuan phylum languages. Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 4, 25-80. SIL archive 37738
sources.note: Phonological features section (3.3, pp. 30-32) covers only the West Papuan languages; tone noted for Abun only. As gets one paragraph (6.1, p. 50: villages Asbakin, Malaumkarta, Mega; ~250 speakers; >60% cognate with Misool lists in Wallace 1869) and a ~13-row comparative wordlist in Appendix E without stress marks. Silent on As stress or tone. (No text; scanned at 200 dpi; PDF served could not be reached by automated download, downloaded from the Internet Archive copy.)
Lists only Kamholz 2014 (pp. 136-137, subclassification comment) and Arnold 2020 (endangerment). No descriptive grammar or phonology exists in Glottolog for As.
